#5327. The downfall of AI’s $5.7 trillion man

The founder and CEO turned Nvidia into the linchpin of the AI boom. Can it survive without him?

In October, in a converted church in West London, Jensen Huang stepped onto a stage to preach to a packed congregation. The then–Nvidia CEO had a gospel to share with the politicians, tech executives, and journalists, Fortune among them, crowding the room: The AI boom was only getting started, and Nvidia was in town to help bankroll it.

“I’m gonna invest in you! I’m gonna invest in you!” he shouted at the founders in the crowd. “We’re not your largest investor, but we are your best investor.”

Huang’s London visit was one stop on a European charm offensive that also swept through France, Sweden, and Germany. At the time, the trip had the feeling of a victory lap. Nvidia is the default supplier of the vital chips that are fueling the AI industry’s rapid growth, and with a market cap that, at one point, topped $5.7 trillion, had seeded an entire ecosystem that came to depend on Nvidia’s support.

If the AI boom is a kind of religion, then Huang had been its high priest—proselytizing to investors and policymakers, ministering to the faithful, and doling out alms to needy startups, AI labs, and neoclouds. Nvidia was the world’s most valuable company, and Huang was one of the world’s most powerful men.

Just three weeks later, that victory lap across Europe looks more like a last hurrah. The man who sold the world his vision of an AI future was soon fighting for his own future—and on Thursday morning, the seismic news broke: Jensen Huang had resigned from his role as CEO.

His abrupt departure followed reports that U.S. intelligence agencies believed Huang had been involved with a woman who was working as a Chinese intelligence asset: Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that had bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips.

For the once seemingly untouchable founder, the fall from grace came fast. Within a week, Huang had sent a memo to Nvidia’s 42,000 staffers acknowledging he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and was “deeply sorry.” Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation; U.S. congressional leaders summoned Huang to answer questions; and federal agencies said they were investigating the matter. Nvidia shares tumbled, and prediction sites began to take bets on whether Huang would resign.

The other shoe dropped when the New York Times reported allegations of a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to Huang. By the next morning, Nvidia’s CEO of 33 years had submitted his resignation. Nvidia’s brief announcement of that fact—and of the appointment of chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO—gave no reason for his departure.

The timing couldn’t have been worse for Nvidia or for the AI industry in which Huang played such a central role. Worries about rising interest rates, dire warnings about AI’s extinction-level risks, and Americans’ opposition to data centers—on display in November’s midterm elections—have already put the AI boom’s foundations on shaky ground.

Critics have long warned that Nvidia’s AI investments had created a risky “circular” web in which Nvidia pours money into AI labs and data center companies, which in turn buy Nvidia chips. The company said that as of the end of July it had invested nearly $50 billion into leading AI model companies alone, including stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic, and Elon Musk’s xAI, and its equity investments across the AI ecosystem totaled twice that amount. The company has increasingly stepped in to use its investment-grade credit to help AI companies and so-called neocloud data center providers obtain financing. In total, it has pledged $170 billion on commitments of this kind, including guarantees valued at $105 billion to OpenAI for just one facility in Ohio. Additionally, Nvidia has been in talks with a consortium of Wall Street lenders to help backstop a $500 billion plan to turn AI chips into tradable securities.

This “central bank of AI” role, as some have characterized it, masked weak demand and inflated a dangerous financial bubble, critics argued. Just as worrisome, it positioned Nvidia as a single point of failure that could destabilize the entire industry. But even the company’s harshest critics didn’t expect the biggest threat to Nvidia to come from the man at the center of it all.

To be clear: Even with its charismatic founder no longer in the CEO role, Nvidia’s core business isn’t going anywhere. Its chips remain the industry standard; its supply is sold out and contracted through the next year. The company can survive “independent of his cult of personality,” says Francine McKenna, an investigative journalist and expert on corporate governance and accounting. But Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners, warns that Nvidia risks losing what made it exceptional: Huang’s willingness to make big bets and keep moving even when some—like Nvidia’s ill-fated effort to make chips for mobile phones—failed. “If they lose that,” he says, “they’re going to become just another chip company.”

Indeed, for all its dominance, Nvidia was never invincible: Some of its best customers were already turning to rival chips or building their own, and governments were pushing for “sovereign AI” that doesn’t depend on American tech.

The AI boom is bigger than any one company, but the sector has yet to prove it can thrive without Nvidia—and Nvidia has yet to prove it can thrive without Huang. Can the industry outgrow its dependence on its most powerful evangelist, or will Huang’s departure from the company he built expose how much of the boom was built on faith?

In a wide-ranging interview with Fortune in London—before news of the affairs broke but months after concerns about Nvidia’s dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed first surfaced—Huang was still going full speed even though he’d only eaten “half of a half sandwich” all day.

He was behind schedule for his next engagement in the church across town, but waved his hand dismissively. “I’ve been late all day,” he said. This was a man who knew very well: The show couldn’t go on without him.

Huang was characteristically optimistic about the future of AI, and about another topic: China. The opportunity there “is large and growing,” he said, wearing his signature black leather jacket in the sweeping lounge of a Central London office building that had just hosted an Nvidia-sponsored hackathon. “We should provide, and we do provide, the best, the soonest, and the most to American companies,” he said. “However, we should compete.”

To understand what happened to Huang, one has to understand Nvidia’s history with China, which has long been a major part of the Santa Clara, Calif.–based company’s business. That business took a hit in 2022 when the Biden administration barred Nvidia from selling its most advanced AI chips there, in an effort to slow Beijing’s progress in the AI race. Successive rule changes forced out even Nvidia’s scaled-down chips. And Beijing started discouraging Chinese AI companies from buying American chips.

Huang—who once publicly complained that U.S. export controls had shrunk Nvidia’s share of China’s AI chip market from 95% to zero—lobbied hard to roll back the export controls. He argued that allowing Nvidia to sell its chips in China would help make American tech the global standard—and crowd out Chinese competitors who were advancing quickly.

When Donald Trump won a second term in 2024, Huang donated $1 million to his inaugural fund and began making frequent pilgrimages to Mar-a-Lago. By all accounts, the two men became close. Trump once phoned while Huang was onstage at a summit in Los Angeles; Huang put him on speaker, and the pair dismissed fears about AI to the crowd.

In late 2025, Huang won a key compromise: Nvidia would be allowed to ship a second-tier chip model to approved Chinese customers. In an unprecedented arrangement, the U.S. government would take a 25% cut.

Huang’s lobbying proved “very effective,” said Ed Mills, a policy analyst with investment firm Raymond James. “There was an ‘in Jensen we trust mantra’ within D.C. and a push within the tech industry to pivot away from seeking to restrict what China got, to seeing if we could get China hooked on our technology.”

It emerged after the scandal broke that Megaspeed had long been suspected of helping Chinese firms dodge export controls. People briefed on U.S. intelligence told the Times that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information on American AI chips and to persuade Nvidia to push for its advanced chips to be sold in China.

China hawks in both U.S. political parties have accused Nvidia of downplaying chip smuggling and overstating the strength of China’s homegrown chips to win looser rules. Huang’s affair with a suspected China asset gave them fresh ammunition to question his motives. “This episode makes clear what we have been alleging the whole time, which is that Nvidia is deeply compromised,” said Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a group that lobbies for regulation of the tech and AI industry. “At best they turned a blind eye to smuggling of their chips into China. At worst, they were complicit in it.”

Meanwhile, China called the allegations “groundless speculation and slander,” and Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe” firm secrets or national security were compromised. (Nvidia did not respond to multiple questions from Fortune seeking additional comment after news of the affairs and eventual resignation.)

Later reporting revealed that a U.S. Commerce Department probe into whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China was halted and passed to the Justice Department after Nvidia’s general counsel contacted the agents running it. An Nvidia spokesperson told the Times that the company had contacted officials “to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field,” and to seek guidance.

Soon after news of Huang’s affair with Alice Huang broke, President Trump called the Nvidia CEO “very aboveboard” but described the situation as “very complex.”

The scandal has also exposed a rift inside the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took to CNBC this week to suggest Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department had stalled efforts to restrict Megaspeed, saying Treasury, Defense, and State had “for months” favored putting the company on the entity list. Bessent said that the focus on Huang’s personal life missed the point. “The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage?” he said.

Reports have also emerged that Bessent had pressed Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over his resistance to export controls (a Commerce spokeswoman later denied this). Alongside Huang, Lutnick has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about the department’s handling of Nvidia chip exports and the Megaspeed case.

At Nvidia’s flagship GPU Technology Conference (GTC) in Berlin a few days after Huang’s London visit, his keynote hit capacity almost two hours before he took the stage. In his speech, Huang was relentlessly upbeat about the AI boom. He urged Europe to embrace its AI future and build more AI “factories”—Huang’s preferred term for data centers. He wrapped the show with a Eurovision song contest performed by AI agents.

But despite Huang’s onstage enthusiasm and his rock-star reception, the AI boom was already showing signs of strain. “He is a cheerleader for a market, and he is cheerleading it,” Paul Miller, a principal analyst at Forrester, said at a crowded Berlin coffee shop after Huang’s event. “But even he’s not blind to the problems that this sector faces.”

Those ranged from concerns about an AI bubble to fears that AI could pose catastrophic risks to humanity. And by November, a new problem had emerged for the industry: the U.S. midterm elections. Democrats, many of whom had campaigned on reining in AI and data center development, won control of Congress, and voters overwhelmingly backed ballot measures aimed at restricting new data centers. AI stocks tumbled following the blue wave elections, as investors braced for a tougher regime of regulation.

Meanwhile, an even more pressing threat to Nvidia is emerging: Its best customers want to build their own AI chips to reduce their costs and to give themselves more control over chip supply.

Google already trains its Gemini models on its own TPU chips instead of relying solely on industry-standard GPUs. Amazon is pushing its Trainium chips. OpenAI is designing its own silicon with Broadcom. Anthropic increasingly uses Google TPUs, AMD’s GPUs, and Amazon’s Trainium chips, too—although it also uses Nvidia’s. AI itself is making it easier for Nvidia’s customers to switch, with developers using frontier AI coding agents to handle the otherwise difficult and time-consuming work of migrating AI workloads between different chip types.

Countries including the U.K. are also trying to develop their own chips and pursuing AI models that might be able to run on “heterodox compute”—which mixes chips of different types in a single data center—to lessen dependency on American tech like Nvidia’s.

This is all bad news for Nvidia. Hyperscalers and large cloud providers account for about half of its data center revenue, which makes up more than 90% of its total sales.

Huang was in Europe in part to play out his defense strategy and counter the continent’s sovereign AI push, pitching Nvidia as the solution: Europeans could run any model they liked, including open-source ones like those from French AI company Mistral, as long as it ran on Nvidia chips. Huang and Nvidia have heavily backed open-source AI, or models whose underlying “weights” are published for anyone to download, modify, and run on their own hardware. (Anthropic and OpenAI, in contrast, keep their weights secret and sell access only through their own apps and cloud services.) The reasoning, for Nvidia: A thriving open-source ecosystem full of companies that need Nvidia chips and its CUDA software to run their models would offer the chipmaker a hedge for if and when the leading closed labs start getting their chips elsewhere. And it’s good for the world, Huang argued in London: “Our business model is so transparent,” he said. “We benefit when the world uses AI. Period. Whether it’s closed or open.”

But not everyone is convinced. Aldo Podestà, CEO of Italian AI startup Giotto.ai, calls Nvidia’s strategy a “Trojan horse.” The company gives away free software that works best on its own chips, he says, so the more people use it, the more they end up relying on Nvidia. “Some dependence is easier to accept when it arrives in the language of freedom,” he says.

Nvidia controls an estimated 80% of the global market for AI chips, and its hardware fills the data centers that tech giants are racing to build. At GTC Berlin, the AI industry’s reliance on Nvidia was on full display.

Beyond the robot demos and packed panels, Nvidia’s partners, including many neocloud companies, took up much of the floor. These newer cloud companies, including Nebius and CoreWeave, buy Nvidia chips in vast quantities, pack them into data centers, and rent the computing power to AI labs and businesses. Many of them count Nvidia as a supplier, an investor, and in some cases, a customer. (Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the center of the recent scandal is also a neocloud.)

As of late July, Nvidia held about $99 billion in investments across what Huang calls AI’s “five-layer cake”: energy companies, data center operators, chipmakers, model builders, and the apps that sit on top. In several cases, those deals come with promises from the labs to spend heavily on Nvidia’s chips.

To Huang, this was all just good business. “Every single one of the layers we’ve selected are very strategic and really high-quality companies to invest in,” Huang said. “Everybody we invest in are connected into Nvidia’s ecosystem, and so we’re making our platform more vibrant.” But to critics like Michael Burry—the investor famed for betting against the U.S. housing bubble—Huang is inflating a dangerous financial bubble in AI with “circular financing” deals.

In his interview with Fortune, Huang dismissed the idea that Nvidia is propping up the AI boom. The company, he said, only takes minority stakes in a given venture, meaning other investors have to believe in the companies, too. He insists that Nvidia’s investments are necessary since AI, unlike earlier software booms, requires enormous amounts of capital upfront. “We’ve created an industry that the VCs alone cannot fund,” he said. And the bets, he added, “have returned fabulously.”

The neoclouds exhibiting in Berlin make a similar case. “If it’s all going to come down to Nvidia’s capital, we would have run out already,” says Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nvidia-backed neocloud Nebius. But even he acknowledges that “many companies out there … have more extreme financial relationships with Nvidia than we do.”

Of course in boom times, the vulnerabilities in the system are easy to ignore. But, McKenna says, “Nvidia’s role propping up much of the AI sector puts enormous pressure on weak links if demand ends up less than the very rosy forecasts.”

The worst case is that several big customers such as OpenAI or CoreWeave can’t earn enough to cover their bills. If that happens, Nvidia could find itself losing chip sales and its equity investment in these companies, and find itself on the hook for some of their debts. Such fallout would cause widespread carnage in the financial markets, starting with Nvidia’s own share price.

It’s worth remembering Cisco, whose routers and switches carried much of the early internet’s traffic. It was a “picks and shovels” operator in the dotcom bubble, holding a place similar to the one Nvidia occupies now—and it too engaged in vendor financing to seed the market for its networking hardware. When the bubble burst in late 2000, Cisco didn’t go out of business. But its market value plunged more than 85%, and to this day, it has never touched those levels again.

“Weak links come from unexpected places and create systemic risks that can ripple through supply chains and sales cycles,” McKenna said in an interview in late October. Now, the vulnerability has emerged at the very center of that web. How far the damage will spread remains to be seen.

It wasn’t just Nvidia’s pile of cash or its investment-grade credit rating or its advanced chips that helped fuel the AI boom: It was also Huang’s good name. Huang was well-regarded long before AI made him a corporate celebrity.

His personal story gave him an underdog credibility few tech billionaires can claim: His first job was as a teenage dishwasher at Denny’s, and he and his cofounders later sketched out the idea for the chip company in one of that restaurant chain’s booths. They founded it in 1993, and Nvidia chips went on to become the go-to for the video gaming industry. Huang steered Nvidia through a near-death experience in its earliest days, when the company almost ran out of money. He built it into the engine of the gaming industry and a Fortune 500 company—then, two decades later, was early to spot the opportunity in artificial intelligence.

If Nvidia is the linchpin of the AI industry, Huang was the linchpin of Nvidia, and his sudden absence exposed just how much of the company’s success rests upon him. In trading following his resignation, Nvidia stock dove as much as 14%, briefly pushing the company below a $4 trillion market cap for the first time in more than a year—then recovering somewhat.

Huang put himself squarely in the middle of a company that still operates “like a startup,” says Laura Fay, who reported directly to Huang for a decade at Nvidia before retiring in July. His management style is famously flat: He has said that at one point he had around 60 direct reports.

That structure helped Nvidia move at what Huang likes to call the “speed of light.” It has also left the company unusually dependent on one man. At the time of his resignation, Nvidia had no president, no chief operating officer, and no obvious No. 2. Its board had no executive chairman.

Nvidia may feel Huang’s absence most acutely in Washington, where he maintained chummy relationships and spent years bending policy in the company’s favor. In May, Trump even brought Huang aboard Air Force One to China—joking at the time to Fortune that he was surprised Huang didn’t have his own private jet. That was reportedly around the same time Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed the president on the suspected spying operation. (Trump has since said that warning “didn’t make much of an impact on” him.)

The company has pushed back hard on think tanks that advocated tougher chip export controls, and some customers, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have avoided taking public positions on the issue for fear of angering the chipmaker, according to a report from The Information. In a statement to the outlet, an Nvidia spokesperson defended the company’s stance against export controls: “America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide.”

Some in the industry have called Nvidia a bully and complained that anyone who disagrees with its stances could be put in “Jensen jail” and cut off from much-needed chips. Others say that clout is just a function of the company’s success: Nvidia “make[s] the best chips, and companies want them a lot and are afraid of doing things that could anger [Nvidia],” says Nathan Calvin, general counsel and VP of state affairs at Encode, a nonprofit that advocates for regulation of AI and Big Tech. “They have a lot of influence and leverage that they can use to advance their favored policy positions.”

It remains to be seen what will happen to that leverage. Huang was Nvidia’s most effective advocate in Washington, and with him gone, the company has lost its loudest voice opposing the tightening of rules on chip sales to China. New export controls are probable, even before the new crop of lawmakers is sworn in. Huang’s departure “guarantees new export controls,” said Raymond James analyst Mills. Three bills proposing new export controls on AI chips and advanced semiconductor equipment are attached to the defense authorization bill awaiting passage on Capitol Hill. The Nvidia scandal “is the accelerant to push [the legislation] over the finish line,” Mills said.

What remains uncertain, he said, is how far those restrictions will go and how robustly the Trump administration will enforce them. The bills still have a loophole for “remote access” in which Chinese AI companies can access Nvidia chips in data centers located in other Asian nations, he noted. That access is exactly what Alice Huang’s former neocloud company, Megaspeed, reportedly provided to Chinese firms. Mills said such loopholes could be closed by policies that would require Nvidia and other chipmakers to implement know-your-customer policies and, in the case of resellers and cloud companies, to identify who their customers’ customers are.

It is also possible that Washington will enact licensing requirements or restrictions on open-source AI models, measures Huang had advocated against. Because the best open-source models have been created by Chinese AI labs, “open-source equals China” in the minds of many lawmakers, Mills said. “If Washington is serious about trying to win the AI race against China we need to see regulations on open-source.”

For investors, policy questions run second to a more immediate one: With Huang gone, who keeps the AI boom intact?

The companies most exposed in the wake of his departure are the neoclouds. The future of all those ventures now looks unclear. Some of Huang’s most ambitious plans to finance these companies, including the more than $500 billion financing platform Nvidia announced with Wall Street firms in August, had already faced resistance at senior levels inside Nvidia, according to Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners. “Nobody at Nvidia could replace Jensen’s role in bringing that together,” he said. Without Huang, he expects many neocloud projects simply won’t get funded.

Following Huang’s exit, investors may also start to scrutinize the numbers Huang used to justify Nvidia’s complex web of investments, said Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business. “Is ‘Jensen’s Math,’ the term used for the complex financial entanglements of these AI firms … about to collapse?” Schloetzer asked rhetorically. “What else has he covered up? What else is lacking candor?”

Nvidia’s partners may also find they have more leverage. Companies that once took Nvidia’s money on Nvidia’s terms could start pushing back. “Maybe they’ll drive a harder bargain,” McKenna said.

The rest of the industry won’t escape unscathed. AI has the momentum to keep going, Goldberg said, but it will become “much more vulnerable to political pressure,” especially amid the backlash against data centers. Anthropic, which is set to go public just days after Nvidia reports its first-ever quarterly earnings without Huang, will be the industry’s first taste of a world after Jensen. Nvidia has agreed to buy about $10 billion of shares as part of a $26 billion private placement alongside the listing, and investors expect that commitment to go ahead without Huang. But his departure could raise the stakes for the wider industry and put some of the companies’ partners under the microscope. Schloetzer, for example, said he expects “much closer scrutiny of [Anthropic’s] ties to Nvidia and customers associated with Nvidia.”

The likely winners are Nvidia’s rival chipmakers. The turmoil, Goldberg says, is “really good for AMD, and it’s really good for Broadcom.” Google’s TPUs are likely to benefit from any concerns about Nvidia’s long-term prospects. AMD, Nvidia’s longtime archrival in the GPU market, will probably see some market share gain, too.

Since the scandal broke, one of the loudest voices in tech has gone quiet. Huang pulled out of public appearances, and his only public statement has been an apology to his staff. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” he wrote. “I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security.”

The chastened tone was a far cry from the bombastic man on the sofa in London. What Huang was selling then was the rosiest possible vision of our AI future. The technology, he argued, would give a small local business the same software firepower as a tech giant. “As a result, everybody will become more ambitious,” he said. “And so I’m excited about that.”

The AI boom has run, in large part, on faith in Jensen Huang and the story he has been telling. He promised that demand for his chips would keep climbing, that AI’s risks could be engineered away, and that the companies building the future-shaping technology could be trusted to police themselves. And for so long, investors, customers, and global leaders happily took that leap with him.

But now that faith has been shattered. The AI boom’s high priest is gone, and the world is waiting to see if the entire AI church he helped construct comes toppling down with him, steeple and all.

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. She's based in Fortune's London office and holds a bachelor’s degree in English from the University of York. You can reach her securely via Signal at beatricenolan.08

Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune, spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI, Fortune’s flagship AI newsletter.

#5325. Your Success Might Be Creating Problems You Can’t See. Here’s What to Ask Yourself.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your business may be growing, but what is that growth really costing you?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In the early 1920s, car manufacturers faced a frustrating problem: They wanted to build more powerful engines, but “engine knocking” kept getting in the way. Fuel igniting unevenly inside an engine created violent vibrations that damaged its components. The finest minds scratched their heads over how to get more power without sacrificing reliability.

Meanwhile, refrigerator manufacturers faced a problem of their own: Some chemicals used in early refrigerators were toxic or highly flammable. A leak could turn a household appliance into a serious hazard. Finding a safer refrigerant could make refrigeration more practical for homes and businesses.

Enter Thomas Midgley Jr., an American engineer who was working at General Motors.

Midgley discovered that adding lead to the fuel could suppress engine knocking. Later, he’d help develop Freon, a refrigerant far less toxic and flammable than many alternatives in use at that time. And just like that, two stubborn engineering problems appeared to be solved.

Manufacturers respected him and adopted his work, and both products became commercial successes. For his work, the American Chemical Society awarded him the Priestley Medal, their highest honor.

You could look at that record and reasonably conclude he had done an excellent job. Entire industries were growing because of him, and he’d earned recognition from his peers.

Would you agree that by the usual measures, Midgley had an extraordinary career? Well … then the other shoe dropped.

Leaded petrol was found to spread toxic lead through the exhaust, exposing generations of people to a metal whose harmful effects we now know better about. Decades after Freon and related chemicals became widespread, scientists discovered that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damaged the Earth’s ozone layer.

Midgley died in 1944, before scientists discovered the damage to the ozone layer. In Midgley’s defence, he could not have predicted every consequence, but his story begs the question for anyone who has built a successful business: What if the very thing that made you successful is also creating costs you haven’t accounted for?

Warning signs around leaded petrol had already appeared during its early production, but the “cost” was ignored, and it remained in widespread use for decades. Freon seemed safe and harmless at first glance, and CFCs were widely used in refrigeration and elsewhere before scientists truly understood how they were damaging the ozone layer.

I think there’s a shared lesson in this about the limits of the original measure of success: A product can work as intended while creating consequences its original purpose never required anyone to consider.

Business owners can fall into a similar pattern. You find something that works, so you do more of it. Being available at all hours helps win customers, so you keep answering calls. Making every important decision helps the business move quickly, so you stay involved as the team expands and you keep accepting work because demand is strong.

Each decision may have solved a problem and helped you get where you are. The costs can emerge later, as the business grows and when you know better.

Early in a company’s life, personal involvement can be exactly what it needs.

The difficulty comes when those habits continue long after the circumstances that made them useful have changed. The founder who once needed to approve every important decision may now be bottlenecking the team. The availability that once won clients leaves no room to switch off. The behavior that helped build the business can become expensive as the business grows.

Sometimes, getting personally involved is exactly what a business needs. You step in, solve a problem, establish a process or build a relationship that gets things moving. But was your involvement meant to be permanent? What began as a short-term solution can quietly become an ongoing responsibility, until you’re spending more time operating the business than leading it.

So now, you have more customers bringing more revenue, but also more complexity. A new market opens up, but demands more travel and attention. The business becomes more profitable while the owner’s time and energy become harder to protect, and their family is neglected.

In my coaching conversations with entrepreneurs, I often return to the difference between what a business produces and what it demands from the person running it. Revenue, profit and growth are easy to track. The cost to a founder’s health, relationships, judgment or freedom can be harder to quantify, so it may go unexamined for years.

A business can be winning by its own measures while the person who built it pays a price they never intended to pay.

None of this is the business owner’s fault, because it’s particularly easy to miss when the numbers look good. A crisis forces you to take a step back and review, but who stops to question continued success? Nobody.

When revenue is growing, and customers are happy, why feel pressured to question the way you’re running the business, even if the arrangement is becoming harder to sustain?

You don’t need to become suspicious of every ambitious decision; building a business requires risk, investment and choices whose consequences cannot be predicted perfectly. But you do need to ask whether your measures of success account for enough of the picture.

Imagine reviewing a new business initiative. You’d probably examine the expected revenue, costs, staffing, return, etc. Would you also ask what it will demand from you personally, what it might displace or whether the business will become more dependent on your involvement?

Tomorrow, choose one part of your business that is performing well. It might be your fastest-growing service, a major client relationship or a process that depends on you being constantly available.

Write down three things: what it produces, what it demands and what it displaces. Then consider whether the arrangement remains sustainable as the business grows. Is it delivering the results you need today at the expense of what the business will need to sustain those results over the longer term? Or can it continue producing the same results without placing increasing demands on you, your team or the resources the business needs elsewhere?

Time spent managing one opportunity is time unavailable for another. Energy spent resolving routine decisions cannot also be spent thinking about the future. An arrangement that works financially may place demands on family life that nobody intended when it began.

Then ask yourself what has changed since you first made that decision. Perhaps the business has grown, your responsibilities have shifted, regulations have changed, or a risk you once considered acceptable now deserves another look. Would you make the same decision today, knowing what you know now?

If the answer is yes, carry on with a clearer understanding of the exchange. If something has changed, you have an opportunity to reconsider the arrangement while you still have options. You might choose to delegate a decision, renegotiate a client relationship or stop doing something that no longer justifies the demands it places on you.

The point is to make that choice while you still have options, rather than waiting for circumstances to make it for you.

You worked hard to build the business you have. You deserve to understand what it gives you, what it asks of you and whether that exchange still makes sense. Success deserves examination even when everything appears to be going well. Sometimes the most important decision a business owner makes is to look beyond the results that got them here.

In the early 1920s, car manufacturers faced a frustrating problem: They wanted to build more powerful engines, but “engine knocking” kept getting in the way. Fuel igniting unevenly inside an engine created violent vibrations that damaged its components. The finest minds scratched their heads over how to get more power without sacrificing reliability.

Meanwhile, refrigerator manufacturers faced a problem of their own: Some chemicals used in early refrigerators were toxic or highly flammable. A leak could turn a household appliance into a serious hazard. Finding a safer refrigerant could make refrigeration more practical for homes and businesses.

Enter Thomas Midgley Jr., an American engineer who was working at General Motors.

#5324. XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:16 pm

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

#5323. You’re Not Behind on AI Agents Yet. Learn How They Work in 10 Minutes, Before Your Competitors Get Ahead

Your competitors are building AI teams. Here’s where to start.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Your competitors may not have hired another employee. They may have built one.

Entrepreneurs are creating custom AI agents to help with marketing, video editing, reporting and scriptwriting while they focus on running their businesses. If you’re still figuring out what an AI agent even does, that can feel intimidating. The good news: It’s not too late to learn. In this video, I break down where to start, what separates an agent from another chatbot and why your first assignment matters more than you might think.

The shift is already underway. In a 2026 G2 survey of 1,019 B2B decision-makers, 66% said their organizations had AI agents running in limited or scaled production. That’s a survey of business software decision-makers, not a measure of every small business. But it’s a sign that agents are moving beyond experiments and into real workflows.

The question for entrepreneurs is where they fit into yours.

Think about everything that happens between an idea and a result. A marketing campaign needs research, a script, content, editing, distribution and a review of what worked. A report needs information gathered and checked before you can make a decision. Each task might seem manageable on its own, but together they can consume the time you wanted to spend growing the business.

AI agents could help take on parts of that work. But giving an agent a job doesn’t automatically mean it will do the right job, understand your standards or know when to ask for your input. That’s where the opportunity and the risk meet.

If you’ve seen my earlier video on ChatGPT’s dots and seven ways entrepreneurs can use them, you’ve already seen how accessible these tools are becoming. The next question is how to turn that access into useful support for your business.

In this video, I share an example from my own work and explore how to identify a worthwhile first job for an agent, without trying to automate your entire business at once. You’ll also see why moving too quickly can create a new bottleneck instead of removing one.

You don’t have to master every AI tool today. But as your competitors learn to build teams that can help them move faster, the work you choose to hand off first could make all the difference.

#5322. Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 1:16 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 1:16 pm

Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.

The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

#5321. Why Tech and Crypto Sold Off After the Blue Wave

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The reversal of the post-election rally offers founders a practical lesson in financing growth, managing risk and separating political expectations from business fundamentals.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The first market reaction to an election can make a poor foundation for a business plan. On Nov. 4, stocks and Bitcoin recovered after the Democratic sweep of Congress. By the next U.S. trading morning, that relief rally was coming apart.

During morning trading on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 4%. Bitcoin also reversed course: Bitcoin.com reported a Bitstamp low of $75,468 by 10:55 a.m. Eastern, after the cryptocurrency had traded above $81,000 the previous day.

The reversal makes a simple political explanation difficult. The election result had not changed. Investors were reassessing what it might mean for businesses and assets whose valuations depended on continued growth, access to financing and confidence in the future.

For entrepreneurs, the useful question is how much of a business plan still works when those assumptions become less generous.

The blue wave introduced another uncertainty for the AI buildout. Reuters reported concern that Democratic victories could bring closer scrutiny of data-center expansion. Chipmakers, data-center operators and companies supplying that expansion came under pressure as investors considered the possibility of slower development.

These were concerns about possible future restrictions. Markets can mark down a company because a project might face delays, long before an agency or legislature acts. Expectations can change a valuation before a rule changes an operating plan.

For a developer, even a temporary delay can change the economics. Equipment has to be financed, contracts carry obligations and interest can accumulate before customers start paying. A project can remain technologically promising while becoming less attractive at its original cost and timetable.

Those concerns were already building before election night. A separate Reuters report described investors questioning returns on enormous AI investments and the use of debt to fund them. The political shift added another uncertainty to that existing debate; it did not create every weakness in the trade.

Company results mattered, too. In its November 4 earnings release, Qualcomm reported quarterly handset revenue of $5.137 billion, down 26% from a year earlier. It also warned of rising semiconductor input costs. These were operating pressures with their own implications for earnings, irrespective of which party won Congress.

For a founder selling an ambitious growth story, that is the uncomfortable part. Investors may still believe in the technology while demanding stronger evidence that expansion will produce an acceptable return.

Bitcoin’s decentralized design does not make its price independent of financial markets. Its network operates without a central owner, but people still buy and sell it with finite capital, changing risk preferences and sometimes borrowed money.

When investors become more defensive, assets with very different underlying purposes can fall together. A trader reducing exposure does not need to abandon a long-term belief in Bitcoin to sell it. The immediate priority may simply be to reduce losses or free up cash.

Leverage can make that process faster. Coinbase International Exchange’s trading rules, for example, provide for automatic liquidation when account equity falls below maintenance requirements. Closing leveraged positions can add further pressure to an existing move. The mechanism helps explain how selling can accelerate without a new piece of political news arriving each time prices fall.

There was evidence of forced closures across crypto. Bitcoin.com cited Coinglass figures showing roughly $839 million in liquidations over the preceding 24 hours, including approximately $741 million in bullish positions. That window spans two trading days, and the figures measure positions liquidated rather than an equivalent amount of cash withdrawn.

The simultaneous sell-off is consistent with investors cutting risk, with leverage amplifying the pressure. It does not establish that the same investors sold both markets, or that the blue wave alone caused Bitcoin’s decline.

The most useful response to this kind of volatility is a closer look at the operating plan. A changing market can reveal dependencies that were easy to overlook when financing was available and valuations were rising.

Start with funding. If the next equity round takes six months longer, which commitments still have to be paid? If a loan becomes more expensive or a project approval takes longer, does the business have enough cash to reach its next meaningful milestone?

Then examine demand. An AI company should be able to show what customers pay for, how often they return and whether delivering the service produces a sustainable margin. A crypto business should understand how lower asset prices, thinner liquidity or increased withdrawals would affect its operations.

Political assumptions deserve the same treatment. An expected approval, friendly administration or proposed law may improve the outlook. Put those benefits in a scenario that can be tested, and identify how the business operates if they arrive later than expected.

This exercise can produce specific decisions: stage a capital project, negotiate more flexible supplier terms or prioritize a product customers already pay to use. It is more useful than trying to predict the next market rebound.

The post-midterm reversal does not settle the long-term case for AI or digital assets. It does show how quickly market enthusiasm can disappear while a company’s spending obligations remain.

The blue wave was part of the context. Earnings, financing costs, expectations for infrastructure growth and leveraged trading also shaped the environment. Assigning the entire move to one election result would leave founders with an incomplete explanation.

A company cannot control the next election or the next wave of selling. It can control how much of its future depends on a favorable outcome. That is where the work should begin.

The first market reaction to an election can make a poor foundation for a business plan. On Nov. 4, stocks and Bitcoin recovered after the Democratic sweep of Congress. By the next U.S. trading morning, that relief rally was coming apart.

During morning trading on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 4%. Bitcoin also reversed course: Bitcoin.com reported a Bitstamp low of $75,468 by 10:55 a.m. Eastern, after the cryptocurrency had traded above $81,000 the previous day.

The reversal makes a simple political explanation difficult. The election result had not changed. Investors were reassessing what it might mean for businesses and assets whose valuations depended on continued growth, access to financing and confidence in the future.

#5320. OfferUp co-founder sees ‘mini power plants’ in buildings full of EVs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 2:41 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 2:41 pm

Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or new power plants built to meet peak demand.

“We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

“Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar said. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”

He described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar said, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5319. ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm

Updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements.

If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The company said the outage was a technical issue, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the company said, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.This was a technical issue…

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna said the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it plans to make to avoid similar outages.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”

We’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Update, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he said.

#5318. Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut

More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.

The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.

Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.)

That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.

The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.

At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.

“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners, which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.

This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.

Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.

With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said.

Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”

Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said.

The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.

“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”

At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.

Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said.

For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.

“If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures, whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.

“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.

She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.

But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”

#5317. Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 13, 2026 at 8:28 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

“I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”

Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion, a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris.

That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came, was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen, who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant, awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

“What’s exciting is seeing this come full circle,” Knowlen said in a 2025 UW story. “Alexis’s passion for this technology grew out of our lab work together, and now we’re collaborating to turn that early research into something that will fly in space.”

During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister, still advises her and the company.

“He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this company,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a new master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and said it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

After finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”

Starting a company comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

“I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she said. “So it made that calculus really easy.”

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she said. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”

That company built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris. Juno wants to play a similar role with a new technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

The first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun said. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”

Building a company has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”

The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she said, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun said, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”

#5316. Startup Founders Are Using AI To File Patents. Here’s Where DIY Becomes A Liability.

Patents can help startups establish competitive advantage, attract investors and protect innovations. But the traditional patent process is expensive, slow and difficult to navigate, particularly for companies with limited resources.

AI is changing that equation. General-purpose tools can research existing patents, document inventions and generate drafts that look like patent applications in minutes. Handling the process themselves can seem like an easy way for founders to save money.

But AI’s capabilities are jagged. AI can perform some tasks remarkably well while missing legal and strategic issues that determine a patent’s commercial value. An application can look sophisticated while providing little meaningful protection.

For example, a patent’s claims define its legal boundaries and what you can stop competitors from doing. Mistakes involving claim scope may remain hidden until an investor, acquirer or competitor scrutinizes the company’s intellectual property.

The question isn’t whether startups should use AI. It’s how much founders can safely do themselves and when legal expertise becomes essential.

Founders can use AI to organize technical documentation, summarize existing patents and identify potentially relevant prior art. Turning engineering notes into an organized invention disclosure, for example, can reduce preparation costs and help counsel focus on strategy.

But the opportunity extends beyond DIY. The right counsel can orchestrate AI across the workflow, coordinating invention discovery, drafting, drawings and quality checks. AI can help counsel explore alternative implementations with the inventors, identify disclosure gaps and check support for claims. Attorneys can direct that work, evaluate the results and connect each step to best protect business needs.

That combination can produce more comprehensive applications with substantially greater efficiency. It is fundamentally different from generating an application with a chatbot and asking a lawyer to review it afterward.

The cheapest filing option is not necessarily the most economical. A poorly prepared application can create false confidence while leaving valuable innovations exposed.

Counsel can help decide what to patent versus maintain as a trade secret, prioritize filings within the company’s budget and assess deadlines before disclosure or filing limits the available options. An internal process that competitors cannot observe or reverse engineer, for example, may be better kept as a trade secret.

Claim scope requires particular judgment. A fraud detection claim tied to one algorithm may leave competitors free to deliver the same functionality using another. Overly broad claims may overlap with existing technology. Valuable claims target what competitors must do to compete. Ideally, a single identifiable competitor can infringe them, and that infringement can be detected and proven.

The specification must describe alternatives and variations that support broader claims later without unnecessarily limiting their scope. AI can assist, but strategic judgment must guide the work.

Filing volume says little about commercial value. Investors and acquirers will look beyond the number of pending applications to ask:

AI’s greatest value is not simply generating more applications at lower costs. It is making meaningful protection more accessible without sacrificing legal judgment.

Founders should ask how a firm coordinates its AI tools and legal expertise, not simply whether it uses AI. The answer should explain how that process improves both efficiency and substance.

Ultimately, the most expensive patent mistake may be discovering too late that a DIY application never adequately protected the innovation on which the business was built.

Michael Drapkin is a founding partner of Landfall IP, an AI-native patent law firm based in Boulder, Colorado. He previously founded one of the largest electronics and computer patent prosecution practices in the U.S. at an Am Law 100 firm and was named U.S. Patent Practitioner of the Year by Managing IP in 2022.

Nathan Mutter is managing partner and founder of Landfall IP, an AI-Native law firm. He has served as top outside counsel at Oura, Coinbase, Rubrik, Salesforce 1 and many others. Mutter pioneered the creation of automation systems and tools that enhance efficiency across all aspects of legal services. His clients include both startups and large public companies.

#5315. Araceli raises $4.5M for drug discovery tools aimed at reducing animal testing

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech company, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health announced $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release.

Araceli said it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, said Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”

Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

The company said that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.
